title: Orpheus et Eurydice
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Hymenaeus comes to the wedding of Orpheus and Eurydice bringing no good sign, and the bride dies of a snakebite while walking in the grass with a crowd of naiads. Orpheus goes down to the Styx and pleads in song before the rulers of the dead; the punished stop being punished, the Furies weep, and Eurydice is given back on one condition. He turns to look, loses her a second time, is refused a second crossing, sits seven days on the bank, and withdraws to the mountains and from the love of women. The last lines make him the first to turn love, among the peoples of Thrace, to boys short of young manhood.

sentences.t:
Inde per inmensum croceo velatus amictu
aethera digreditur Ciconumque Hymenaeus ad oras
tendit et Orphea nequiquam voce vocatur.
sentences.l: Thence through the measureless upper air, veiled in a saffron cloak, Hymenaeus departs, and toward the shores of the Cicones he makes his way, and is called by the voice of Orpheus in vain.
sentences.i: From there Hymen goes off through the boundless sky, wrapped in his saffron cloak, and heads for the coasts of the Cicones — summoned, and for nothing, by the voice of Orpheus.
sentences.n: digreditur is deponent: passive in form, active in sense, “he departs”. Orphea is an adjective, “Orphean”, agreeing with voce — the voice is Orpheus'. per inmensum has its adjective in line 1 and its noun aethera at the head of line 2, so the span of sky is stretched across the line-end. The saffron cloak is the wedding god's own colour, and nequiquam, “to no purpose”, stands before the verb that reports the summons.

sentences.t:
Adfuit ille quidem, sed nec sollemnia verba
nec laetos vultus nec felix attulit omen.
sentences.l: He was there, indeed — but he brought neither the ceremonial words nor glad looks nor a favourable omen.
sentences.i: He came, true enough; but he brought no ritual words, no glad face, no lucky omen.
sentences.n: quidem concedes the point that sed then takes away: he came, yes, and that is all. Three nec phrases share the single verb attulit, so the refusals are stacked and one verb serves them all. sollemnia verba are the set words of the ceremony, and a felix omen is a favourable one, felix in its older sense of fruitful rather than happy.

sentences.t:
Fax quoque, quam tenuit, lacrimoso stridula fumo
usque fuit nullosque invenit motibus ignes.
sentences.l: The torch too, the one he held, was sputtering all the while with tear-drawing smoke, and found no flames by its shaking.
sentences.i: The torch he carried sputtered the whole time in smoke that stung the eyes, and no amount of waving would bring it to a flame.
sentences.n: quoque here is the adverb “too”, not quo-que, “and with which”. stridula is the hiss of a torch that will not catch; lacrimoso fumo is smoke that makes the eyes water. motibus is instrumental — the shaking meant to fan it — and invenit, “found”, treats the flame as something that has to be looked for. A wedding torch that will not burn is a sign, not a mishap.

sentences.t:
Exitus auspicio gravior: nam nupta per herbas
dum nova naiadum turba comitata vagatur,
occidit in talum serpentis dente recepto.
sentences.l: The outcome was graver than the sign: for while the new bride, attended by a throng of naiads, was wandering through the grass, she fell dead, a serpent's tooth taken into her ankle.
sentences.i: What followed was worse than the omen: for as the new bride roamed through the grass with a crowd of naiads about her, she died of a snake's fang in her ankle.
sentences.n: gravior is a comparative with a bare ablative of comparison, auspicio — heavier than the omen. comitata is the participle of the deponent comitor used passively, “accompanied by”, agreeing with nupta. dente recepto is an ablative absolute, literally “the tooth having been taken in”, so the bite arrives in Latin as something received rather than as something the snake does, and in talum, “into her ankle”, depends on that participle. occidit is the plain verb for falling dead, and the sentence gives the snake no verb of its own.

sentences.l: And after the Rhodopeian bard had wept for her enough to the airs above, so that he should not fail to try the shades as well, he dared to go down to the Styx by the Taenarian gate;
sentences.i: When the bard of Rhodope had mourned her long enough under the open sky, he dared — so as not to leave even the shades untried — to go down to the Styx by the gate at Taenarus;
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative, “and her”, opening the sentence as the object of deflevit. ne non temptaret is a purpose clause with a double negative, “lest he should not try”, so the point is a refusal to leave anything untried. ad superas auras is the upper air, the world of the living, and it is where the weeping is done. ausus est belongs to a semi-deponent verb, passive in form and active in sense: he dared. Rhodopeius is the adjective of a Thracian mountain, standing in for his name.

sentences.t:
perque leves populos simulacraque functa sepulcro
Persephonen adiit inamoenaque regna tenentem
umbrarum dominum.
sentences.l: and through the weightless peoples and the phantoms that have discharged their burial, he came to Persephone and to the lord of the shades who holds the joyless kingdoms.
sentences.i: and through the insubstantial crowds and the ghosts who have gone through their funeral rites, he came before Persephone and the lord of the shades, who rules that unlovely kingdom.
sentences.n: leves populos are the “light” dead, weightless because they have no body. functa is the perfect participle of the deponent fungor, which governs an ablative and is active in sense: simulacra functa sepulcro are shades that have discharged the duty of burial and so have a right to be where they are. inamoena is a negative compound, “not pleasing”. The participle tenentem closes line 15 and the phrase it agrees with, umbrarum dominum, opens line 16 — and that phrase is all the naming the text gives him.

sentences.t:
Pulsisque ad carmina nervis
sic ait:
sentences.l: And with the strings struck to his song, he spoke thus:
sentences.i: And striking the strings to his song, he spoke:
sentences.n: pulsis ... nervis is an ablative absolute, “the strings having been struck”, where English wants a clause with a subject. nervi are the gut strings of the lyre, and ad carmina is “to match the song”. What follows is laid out as an argument, and the instrument is part of the delivery.

sentences.t:
“O positi sub terra numina mundi,
in quem reccidimus, quidquid mortale creamur,
si licet et falsi positis ambagibus oris
vera loqui sinitis,
sentences.l: O powers of the world set beneath the earth, into which we fall back, whatever mortal thing we are created — if it is permitted, and you allow true things to be spoken with the evasions of a lying mouth laid aside,
sentences.i: You powers of the world laid under the earth, the world we all drop back into, all of us that are made mortal — if it is allowed, and you let a man speak the truth with no lying roundabout,
sentences.n: positi agrees with mundi, not with numina: it is the world that is set beneath the earth. in quem picks up mundi, and reccidimus is re-cado, to fall back — we return to where we came from. quidquid mortale creamur is an internal accusative with a first-person plural passive, “whatever mortal thing we are created”, that is, all of us in so far as we are born to die. positis ambagibus oris falsi is an ablative absolute; ambages are an orator's evasions, and the opening promises plain speech before the case is begun.

sentences.t:
non huc, ut opaca viderem
Tartara, descendi, nec uti villosa colubris
terna Medusaei vincirem guttura monstri:
sentences.l: I did not come down here in order to see dark Tartarus, nor to bind the three throats, shaggy with snakes, of the Medusan monster:
sentences.i: I have not come down here to look at the darkness of Tartarus, nor to put chains on the three snake-shaggy throats of that Medusa-like monster.
sentences.n: Two purpose clauses, ut ... viderem and uti ... vincirem, deny two motives before the true one is given — the shape of a speaker clearing away what he expects to be suspected of. villosa colubris is “shaggy with snakes”, an ablative of respect; terna is the distributive numeral, “three apiece”. opaca stands in line 20 and the noun it belongs to, Tartara, opens line 21, so the adjective reaches its noun across the line-break. The monster is not named: Medusaei makes it snake-haired like Medusa, and the three throats do the identifying.

sentences.t:
causa viae est coniunx, in quam calcata venenum
vipera diffudit crescentesque abstulit annos.
sentences.l: the cause of my journey is my wife, into whom a viper, trodden underfoot, poured out its venom and carried off her growing years.
sentences.i: My wife is the reason for the road I have taken: a viper she trod on emptied its poison into her and took away the years she still had coming.
sentences.n: causa viae est is the plainest statement of a case: here is my reason. calcata is a passive participle agreeing with vipera — the snake is the one trodden on, so the Latin puts the accident on the snake's side of the sentence rather than hers. in quam is a relative reaching back to coniunx and is governed by diffudit. crescentes annos are the years that were still increasing: not the life she had, but the life she had not reached.

sentences.t:
Posse pati volui nec me temptasse negabo:
vicit Amor.
sentences.l: I wished to be able to endure it, and I shall not deny that I made the attempt: Love won.
sentences.i: I wanted to be able to bear it, and I will not deny I tried. Love won.
sentences.n: posse pati stacks two infinitives under volui: what he wanted was the capacity to endure, not simply to endure. temptasse is the syncopated perfect infinitive of temptare in an accusative and infinitive after negabo, with me as its subject, “that I tried”. vicit Amor is two words and a full stop, and Amor is capitalised in the edition, so it is the god who wins the point, not a feeling.

sentences.t:
Supera deus hic bene notus in ora est,
an sit et hic, dubito.
sentences.l: In the region above, this god is well known; whether he is here as well, I am unsure.
sentences.i: Up in the world above, this god is well known. Whether he is here too, I do not know.
sentences.n: supera ... in ora, “in the upper region”, has its adjective separated from its noun by the whole clause. hic in the first clause is the demonstrative, “this god”; hic in the second is the adverb, “here” — the same four letters doing two jobs one after the other. an sit is an indirect question with the subjunctive after dubito.

sentences.l: But even here, all the same, I read the signs that he is; and if the report of the old carrying-off has not lied, Love joined you two as well.
sentences.i: But here too, all the same, I take it he is. And if the story of that old abduction has not lied, then Love brought the pair of you together as well.
sentences.n: auguror is deponent, active in sense: to read the signs, to take it that something is so. mentita is likewise deponent, perfect passive in shape and active in meaning, “has lied”. rapina is the plain word for a carrying-off by force, and Orpheus offers it as hearsay he will not vouch for — si ... non est mentita — while asking the two he is addressing to accept it as a marriage that Love made. The Latin does not narrate the event; it is left at the one word.

sentences.t:
Per ego haec loca plena timoris,
per chaos hoc ingens vastique silentia regni,
Eurydices, oro, properata retexite fata.
sentences.l: By these places full of dread, by this huge void and the silences of the waste kingdom: unweave, I beg you, the hurried fate of Eurydice.
sentences.i: By these places full of fear, by this vast emptiness and the silence of your desolate kingdom: unravel, I beg you, the fate that was hurried on Eurydice.
sentences.n: Per ego haec loca is the formula of a solemn adjuration with the pronoun forced inside it: the oath is per ... haec loca, and ego is wedged in after the preposition. oro sits inside the request itself rather than in front of it. Eurydices is a Greek genitive. retexere is texere run backwards, to unweave what has been woven, so a fate is treated as cloth that can be unpicked; properata says it was hurried forward before its time.

sentences.t:
Omnia debemur vobis, paulumque morati
serius aut citius sedem properamus ad unam.
sentences.l: We are all of us owed to you; and having lingered a little, later or sooner we hurry to one same dwelling.
sentences.i: We are all owed to you. After a short delay, sooner or later, we hurry to a single home.
sentences.n: Omnia debemur is a deliberate mismatch: the neuter plural omnia, “all things”, stands with a first-person plural passive, debemur, “we are owed”. English cannot keep both at once, so the literal spreads it as “we are all of us owed”. The verb is the language of debt, and the dative vobis is the creditor. morati is the participle of the deponent moror, active in sense, “having delayed”. Ovid writes serius aut citius, later before sooner, the reverse of the English pairing.

sentences.t:
Tendimus huc omnes, haec est domus ultima, vosque
humani generis longissima regna tenetis.
sentences.l: We all make for this place; this is the last house; and you hold the longest-lasting kingdoms over the human race.
sentences.i: We are all headed here. This is the final house, and you hold the longest-lasting rule there is over the human race.
sentences.n: Three short clauses, each conceding a premise before the request is renewed. domus ultima is the last house a person moves to. longissima is longest in duration, not in extent: the dead are held longer than the living are. humani generis is a genitive attached to regna — a rule over the human race, not a realm made of it. tenetis is the same verb that appeared in its participle, tenentem, of the lord of the shades at line 15.

sentences.t:
Haec quoque, cum iustos matura peregerit annos,
iuris erit vestri: pro munere poscimus usum.
sentences.l: This woman too, when ripe she has completed her lawful years, will be of your right: in place of an outright gift we ask the use.
sentences.i: She too, once she has come to ripeness and run out her lawful years, will fall under your jurisdiction. Instead of an outright gift, we ask for the use of her.
sentences.n: iuris erit vestri is a genitive of right: she will fall within your jurisdiction, and the phrasing is legal rather than sentimental. matura, agreeing with her, is “ripe”, the word for fruit ready to fall, and iustos annos are the years due to her. The last four words are the plea in miniature and are drawn from property law — munus is an outright gift that transfers ownership, usus is the right to use a thing that belongs to another. He asks to borrow her, not to keep her, and poscimus is first person plural, keeping the plea inside the same “we” the argument has used since Omnia debemur.

sentences.t:
Quod si fata negant veniam pro coniuge, certum est
nolle redire mihi: leto gaudete duorum.”
sentences.l: But if the fates refuse the indulgence on my wife's behalf, it is settled for me not to wish to return: take your joy in the death of two.
sentences.i: But if the fates refuse this concession for my wife, my mind is made up: I do not want to go back. Enjoy the death of two.
sentences.n: venia is a formal indulgence, the concession a magistrate or a court grants, and pro coniuge is “on my wife's behalf”, the phrase an advocate uses of a client. certum est ... mihi is impersonal with a dative and takes the infinitive nolle — not “I refuse to return” but “it is fixed for me not to want to”. gaudete is a bare imperative aimed at the gods: if they will not return one life, they may have two deaths. The speech ends on duorum, the number, with nothing after it.

sentences.t:
Talia dicentem nervosque ad verba moventem
exsangues flebant animae:
sentences.l: As he said such things and moved the strings to his words, the bloodless souls wept for him:
sentences.i: While he spoke so and moved the strings to his words, the bloodless souls were weeping for him.
sentences.n: dicentem and moventem are two accusative participles with no noun to hang on: the object of flebant is “him, saying such things and moving the strings”, and Latin can leave the pronoun out entirely. flere is transitive here — to weep for someone. exsangues, “without blood”, is the standing description of the dead, since what they lack is blood and so a body.

sentences.t:
nec Tantalus undam
captavit refugam, stupuitque Ixionis orbis,
sentences.l: Tantalus did not catch at the water that flees him, and the wheel of Ixion stood struck still,
sentences.i: Tantalus stopped snatching at the water that always retreats, and Ixion's wheel halted in astonishment,
sentences.n: captavit is the frequentative of capere: not one grab but the endless repeated grabbing that is the punishment. refugam is an adjective, “fleeing back”, of water that recedes as he stoops to it — undam ends line 41 and refugam does not arrive until line 42. stupuit is used of a person struck motionless with amazement and is given here to a wheel, so the machine stops as a listener would. Both names are dropped in without explanation.

sentences.t:
nec carpsere iecur volucres, urnisque vacarunt
Belides, inque tuo sedisti, Sisyphe, saxo.
sentences.l: nor did the birds tear at the liver, and the daughters of Belus were idle from their urns, and you sat, Sisyphus, on your stone.
sentences.i: the birds left off tearing at the liver, the daughters of Belus had a rest from their jars, and you, Sisyphus, sat down on your stone.
sentences.n: carpsere is the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for -erunt, and vacarunt is a syncopated vacaverunt: both save a syllable. urnis is an ablative of separation with vacarunt — they were free of, at leisure from, their jars. The text does not say whose liver the birds tear. In the last clause Ovid turns aside and speaks to one of the punished directly — sedisti, “you sat” — an apostrophe that lifts a single figure out of the list, and inque tuo ... saxo wraps the address inside the phrase.

sentences.t:
Tunc primum lacrimis victarum carmine fama est
Eumenidum maduisse genas.
sentences.l: Then for the first time, the report is, the cheeks of the Eumenides, overcome by his song, grew wet with tears.
sentences.i: Then for the first time — so the story runs — the Furies were beaten by his song, and their cheeks were wet with tears.
sentences.n: fama est governs an accusative and infinitive, genas ... maduisse, “that their cheeks grew wet”. victarum is a passive participle in the genitive agreeing with Eumenidum, not with genas: it is they, and not their cheeks, that are overcome, and carmine is the ablative of what overcame them. Eumenides, “the kindly ones”, is the placating name for the Furies, and it is the name the poem uses at the moment they weep. Tunc primum marks the thing as unprecedented, and fama est keeps the poet from vouching for it.

sentences.t:
Nec regia coniunx
sustinet oranti nec qui regit ima negare,
Eurydicenque vocant.
sentences.l: Nor does the royal wife bring herself, nor he who rules the depths, to refuse the man pleading; and they call Eurydice.
sentences.i: Neither the queen nor the ruler of the depths can bear to refuse the man who is pleading, and they call for Eurydice.
sentences.n: sustinet is “to bear to do a thing”, with the infinitive negare held back to the end of line 47: they cannot bear to say no. oranti is a dative participle used as a noun, “to the man pleading”, depending on negare. qui regit ima is again a relative clause standing in for a name the poem does not give. The verb is singular for the two refusals taken one at a time, and plural, vocant, for the single act they do together.

sentences.t:
Umbras erat illa recentes
inter et incessit passu de vulnere tardo.
sentences.l: She was among the newly-arrived shades, and she came forward with a step slow from the wound.
sentences.i: She was among the shades newly come, and she walked forward with a step the wound had made slow.
sentences.n: inter is postponed behind both its own noun and the subject: umbras erat illa recentes inter, “among the recent shades”. de vulnere is causal, giving the reason for the slowness — a shade still carries the injury that killed it, and that detail is the whole point of the clause. incessit is the verb for a measured walking-in rather than for ordinary going.

sentences.t:
Hanc simul et legem Rhodopeius accipit Orpheus,
ne flectat retro sua lumina, donec Avernas
exierit valles: aut inrita dona futura.
sentences.l: Her, and at the same time a condition, Rhodopeian Orpheus receives: that he should not bend his eyes back until he has gone out from the Avernan valleys; otherwise the gift would be void.
sentences.i: Orpheus of Rhodope receives her, and with her a condition: that he not turn his eyes back until he has left the valleys of Avernus — otherwise the gift will come to nothing.
sentences.n: Hanc simul et legem yokes a person and a term of contract to one verb, accipit: he takes delivery of both at once. lex here is a clause in an agreement, not a law of nature. ne flectat is the stipulation itself, a negative clause hanging on legem — that he not bend his eyes back — and exierit is a future perfect after donec, so the term is set out with legal exactness. The sentence closes with esse left out: inrita dona futura, “the gifts about to be void”, a bare future participle with no verb beside it. Magnus prints Orpheus in line 50; some editions print heros, “the hero”.

sentences.t:
Carpitur acclivis per muta silentia trames,
arduus, obscurus, caligine densus opaca.
sentences.l: The climbing path is taken through mute silences — steep, dark, thick with murky gloom.
sentences.i: The upward track is picked out through unbroken silence: steep, dark, choked with heavy fog.
sentences.n: carpitur is passive with the doer left out — the path “is taken”, and Latin need not say by whom, though both of them are on it. carpere viam is the ordinary idiom for making one's way. muta silentia is a plural for a single silence, and a silence called mute is deliberate excess. The three adjectives of line 54 are set down with no connective between them, and caligine ... opaca is an ablative of respect with densus.

sentences.t: Nec procul afuerunt telluris margine summae:
sentences.l: And they were not far away from the rim of the topmost earth:
sentences.i: They were not far now from the edge of the upper world:
sentences.n: afuerunt is the perfect of absum with an ablative of separation, margine — “were distant from the edge”. summae telluris is the earth's surface named as its highest part, which is how it stands to someone climbing towards it. The verb is plural and covers the two of them — the first verb since the descent to take both of them as its subject.

sentences.t:
hic, ne deficeret, metuens avidusque videndi
flexit amans oculos;
sentences.l: here, fearing that she might be failing, and greedy for the sight of her, the lover turned his eyes;
sentences.i: there, afraid she was giving out, and hungry to see her, the lover turned his eyes;
sentences.n: ne deficeret is a fear clause after metuens; its subject is not expressed, and the natural one is she — deficere is to give out, to fail on the way. avidus videndi takes an objective genitive of the gerund, “greedy of seeing”. amans is not a participle used adjectivally but the noun, “the lover”, and it is the subject of flexit — at the moment of the mistake the Latin names him by the thing that causes it. flexit oculos is a bending of the eyes, not a turning of the body.

sentences.t:
et protinus illa relapsa est,
bracchiaque intendens prendique et prendere certans
nil nisi cedentes infelix arripit auras.
sentences.l: and at once she slipped back, and stretching out his arms, straining both to be caught and to catch, the unhappy man seizes nothing but the yielding air.
sentences.i: and at once she slid back down; and reaching out his arms, straining to be caught and to catch her, he seized, poor man, nothing but the air giving way.
sentences.n: prendi et prendere sets the same verb passive and then active under one participle, certans: he strains to be caught and to catch. intendens, certans and infelix are all masculine, so the arms and the straining are his — the Latin does not give the reaching to her. cedentes is the participle of cedere, air that gives way as it is grasped. relapsa est is perfect and arripit present, so the loss is reported and the grab is put in front of us as it happens.

sentences.t:
Iamque iterum moriens non est de coniuge quicquam
questa suo: quid enim nisi se quereretur amatam?
sentences.l: And now, dying a second time, she made no complaint at all about her husband: for what was she to complain of, except that she had been loved?
sentences.i: And now, dying a second time, she made no complaint against her husband — what was there to complain of, except that she had been loved?
sentences.n: questa est is the perfect of the deponent queror, passive in shape and active in sense: she complained, and here she did not. de coniuge suo is the thing complained about. se ... amatam is an accusative and infinitive with esse left out, the object of quereretur. quereretur is a deliberative subjunctive in a question — what was she to complain of? — and moriens is a present participle, so the second death is going on as the words are spoken.

sentences.t:
Supremumque “vale,” quod iam vix auribus ille
acciperet, dixit revolutaque rursus eodem est.
sentences.l: And she said a last “farewell”, which he could now scarcely take in with his ears, and she was rolled back again to the same place.
sentences.i: And she said a last goodbye — one he could barely catch by now — and was carried back again to where she had come from.
sentences.n: quod ... acciperet is a relative clause with the subjunctive of characteristic: the farewell was of a kind he could scarcely hear. auribus is an instrumental ablative spelled out where English would drop it — he takes it in with his ears. ille closes line 62 and its verb acciperet opens line 63, so the hearing is held over by the line-break. revoluta est is passive: she does not go back, she is rolled back. supremum is the adjective used of last things — last words, last day.

sentences.t:
Non aliter stupuit gemina nece coniugis Orpheus,
quam tria qui timidus, medio portante catenas,
colla canis vidit,
sentences.l: Orpheus was struck no otherwise by the twin death of his wife than the frightened man who saw the three necks of the dog, the middle one carrying chains,
sentences.i: Orpheus was stunned by his wife's second death exactly as the terrified man was who saw the dog's three necks, the middle one in chains,
sentences.n: Non aliter ... quam opens a comparison that runs for four lines. gemina nece is an ablative of cause, “by a twofold death”. tria comes early in line 65 and colla, the noun it counts, opens line 66, with the relative and an ablative absolute, medio portante catenas, wedged between them — so the number arrives first, then the interruption, then the necks. The dog is not named, and qui timidus is a relative with no antecedent, “the man who”, for a figure the poem expects to be known.

sentences.t:
quem non pavor ante reliquit,
quam natura prior, saxo per corpus oborto;
sentences.l: whom fear did not leave before his earlier nature did, with stone rising up over his body;
sentences.i: and fear did not leave him until his own nature left him first, as stone came up over his body;
sentences.n: non ... ante ... quam is antequam split in two, “not before”: fear left him only at the moment his nature did. natura prior is the nature he had before the change, and the change itself is reported by the ablative absolute saxo per corpus oborto, “stone having risen up over his body”, of something coming up from below. The Latin says a man was frightened into stone and never says who he was.

sentences.t:
quique in se crimen traxit voluitque videri
Olenos esse nocens,
sentences.l: and Olenos, who drew the charge onto himself and wanted to be seen to be the guilty one,
sentences.i: and Olenos, who took the blame on himself and wanted to be thought the guilty party,
sentences.n: crimen in se traxit is courtroom language — to draw an accusation onto oneself, to take a charge. videri ... nocens is “to be seen to be doing harm”, with the present participle of noceo standing as the predicate. The clause begins in line 68 and the name Olenos does not arrive until the head of line 69, after the deed has been described.

sentences.t:
tuque, o confisa figurae,
infelix Lethaea, tuae, iunctissima quondam
pectora, nunc lapides, quos umida sustinet Ide.
sentences.l: and you, o unhappy Lethaea, who trusted in your form — hearts once most closely joined, now stones, which watery Ida holds up.
sentences.i: and you, poor Lethaea, who put your trust in your own looks: two hearts once bound as close as could be, now stones, held up by wet Ida.
sentences.n: tuque ... o confisa is apostrophe, the poet turning aside to speak to a figure in his own story. confisa is the participle of the semi-deponent confido, active in sense, “having trusted”, and it takes a dative: figurae closes line 69 and tuae, which agrees with it, waits until line 70. iunctissima pectora, “hearts most joined”, stands in apposition to the pair, and nunc lapides is the same pair after the change, set beside it with no verb between the two states. The lines do not say why the trust in her own form was an offence.

sentences.t:
Orantem frustraque iterum transire volentem
portitor arcuerat.
sentences.l: As he pleaded and wished in vain to cross a second time, the ferryman had kept him off.
sentences.i: He begged, and wanted to cross a second time, and got nowhere: the ferryman had barred him.
sentences.n: Orantem and volentem are again accusative participles with no noun — the object of arcuerat is “him, pleading and wanting”. arcuerat is pluperfect, so the refusal is reported as already settled before the sentence starts. frustra goes with volentem, so it is the wanting rather than the crossing that comes to nothing. portitor is the toll-taker at a crossing, the usual word for the ferryman of the dead, and the poem does not name him.

sentences.t:
Septem tamen ille diebus
squalidus in ripa Cereris sine munere sedit:
cura dolorque animi lacrimaeque alimenta fuere.
sentences.l: Yet for seven days he sat on the bank, unwashed, without the gift of Ceres: care and grief of heart and tears were his nourishment.
sentences.i: Even so, he sat on the bank for seven days, unwashed and without bread: worry, heartsickness and tears were what he lived on.
sentences.n: septem diebus is an ablative of time used for a stretch of duration. squalidus is the state of a mourner, unwashed and unkempt, and it is the standing word for that condition rather than for dirt as such. Cereris munus is bread named by the goddess who gives grain, so sine munere means he did not eat. Three subjects — cura, dolor, lacrimae — take one plural verb and one predicate noun, alimenta, so grief occupies the place food should. fuere is the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for -erunt.

sentences.t:
Esse deos Erebi crudeles questus, in altam
se recipit Rhodopen pulsumque aquilonibus Haemum.
sentences.l: Having complained that the gods of Erebus were cruel, he withdraws himself to high Rhodope and to Haemus, beaten by the north winds.
sentences.i: Complaining that the gods of Erebus were cruel, he took himself off to high Rhodope and to Haemus, where the north winds beat.
sentences.n: questus is once more the deponent participle of queror, active in sense, “having complained”, and it governs the accusative and infinitive esse deos ... crudeles, which the Latin puts in front of it. se recipit is the reflexive idiom for withdrawing — he takes himself back. The verb is present after a perfect participle, the historic present carrying the retreat. pulsum agrees with Haemum: the mountain is struck by the aquilones, the northerlies.

sentences.t:
Tertius aequoreis inclusum piscibus annum
finierat Titan,
sentences.l: The third Sun had brought to a close the year shut in by the fishes of the sea,
sentences.i: The Sun had closed the third year, the year that is shut in by the Fishes of the sea,
sentences.n: Titan is the Sun. tertius agrees with him rather than with the year, though what is third is the year — Latin can hang the ordinal on the agent and leave the counting to the reader. inclusum agrees with annum, and aequoreis piscibus is the ablative that bounds it: the year is shut in by the sign of the Fishes, which closes the zodiac's round. finierat is pluperfect, so the sentence dates what follows rather than narrating it.

sentences.t:
omnemque refugerat Orpheus
femineam venerem, seu quod male cesserat illi,
sive fidem dederat.
sentences.l: and Orpheus had fled from all love of women, whether because it had gone badly for him, or because he had given his word.
sentences.i: and Orpheus had kept away from women's love altogether — either because it had turned out badly for him, or because he had given a pledge.
sentences.n: femineam venerem is the love of women, venus in the plain sense of sexual love; omnem is separated from its noun venerem by the verb, the subject and the line-end. refugerat is pluperfect like finierat, so this is his settled state by the time the third year is out. seu ... sive sets two reasons side by side and settles on neither. male cesserat is impersonal, “it had gone badly”, with the dative illi, and fidem dederat is to give one's word — the lines do not say to whom.

sentences.t:
Multas tamen ardor habebat
iungere se vati, multae doluere repulsae.
sentences.l: Yet a burning held many women to join themselves to the bard; many, turned away, grieved.
sentences.i: All the same, many women burned to join themselves to the singer, and many grieved at being refused.
sentences.n: ardor habebat multas with the infinitive iungere is an unusual construction — a burning that “held” them to the doing of a thing — and se in iungere se refers to the women, not to the bard. repulsae is a passive participle agreeing with multae: they were pushed back. doluere is the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for -erunt. The women are counted twice, multas and multae, once as wanting and once as refused.

sentences.t:
Ille etiam Thracum populis fuit auctor amorem
in teneros transferre mares citraque iuventam
aetatis breve ver et primos carpere flores.
sentences.l: He too was the one who began it for the peoples of the Thracians: to transfer love to tender males, and, on the near side of young manhood, to pluck the brief spring of their age and its first flowers.
sentences.i: He was also the one who started it among the peoples of Thrace: turning love to tender boys, and, before young manhood, picking the short spring of their years and the first of their flowers.
sentences.n: fuit auctor with two infinitives, transferre and carpere, is “he was the one who began the practice of”: auctor is the word for the originator of a thing. Thracum populis is a dative of the people it was begun for. teneros mares are males still young, and citra iuventam puts them on the near side of iuventa, young manhood, that is, short of it. The last line is metaphor throughout — breve ver aetatis is the short spring of a life, and carpere is the ordinary verb for picking flowers or fruit, used here of the boys.
